theme: The throne room; the Lamb takes the scroll
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 4:1-5:14. John is taken up into the throne room of heaven. Notice the worship around the throne, the sealed scroll, the weeping that turns to praise, and the surprising appearance of the Lamb.
settingTheScene: After the letters to the churches, John is invited through an open door into heaven, where the rest of the book is seen from the perspective of the throne. The scene recalls Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1, and Daniel 7. The throne is the central fact of the universe, and the question of Revelation 4 and 5 is: who is worthy to carry out God’s plan for history, as symbolized in the scroll? For persecuted Christians who feel that Caesar holds power, this is the vision they need.
observation: “At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne” (4:2).
“Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” (4:8).
“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things” (4:11).
“Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (5:5).
“A Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6).
“For you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (5:9).
“Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!” (5:12).
“To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” (5:13).
interpretation:
John is called up through an open door and immediately is in the Spirit before a throne. The one seated on it is described only in terms of gemstones, jasper and carnelian, with a rainbow like an emerald around it. He is not described in human form, because he is beyond description. Around the throne are twenty-four elders on thrones, dressed in white with golden crowns, probably representing the whole people of God (the twelve tribes and twelve apostles). Lightning and thunder come from the throne. Before it burn seven torches, which are the seven spirits of God, and there is a sea of glass like crystal. Four living creatures, full of eyes, like the seraphim of Isaiah 6, never cease to say: “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” When they give glory, the elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne, saying: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.” Heaven’s first act is worship of the Creator.

In chapter 5, John sees in the right hand of the one on the throne “a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals.” This is a scroll of God’s purposes for the world, a will or deed that must be opened for its judgments and blessings to come to pass. A mighty angel asks, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?” No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth is found worthy. John weeps loudly. If no one can open it, God’s purposes for history, for his people, and for creation cannot be carried out. But an elder says, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

John listens for the Lion, but when he looks, he sees “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.” He heard “Lion” and saw “Lamb.” This is the central image of the book: Christ conquers by sacrifice, through his death. He bears the marks of slaughter but stands alive. His seven horns signify complete power, and his seven eyes complete knowledge. He takes the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne, and the whole of heaven erupts in a new song: “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”

Then the circle of praise widens: myriads of angels, “ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands,” saying with a loud voice: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!” And finally every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea: “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” The four living creatures say “Amen,” and the elders fall down and worship. The Lamb shares the worship given to the one on the throne. This is the best answer to the question of what Revelation is about: the Lamb who was slain holds the scroll of history.
connection: Isaiah 6:1-4 and Ezekiel 1 are the sources for the throne and the creatures. Daniel 7:9-10 shows the Ancient of Days enthroned. Genesis 49:9-10 is the background of the Lion of Judah, and Isaiah 11:1, 10 of the Root of David. Isaiah 53:7 and John 1:29 speak of the Lamb. Exodus 12 is the Passover lamb. Daniel 12:4 and Ezekiel 2:9-10 mention sealed scrolls. Philippians 2:9-11 describes every creature confessing Christ. Colossians 1:15-20 describes his supremacy. Ephesians 1:9-10 speaks of God’s plan for the fullness of time. Revelation 1:5-6 uses the same kingdom and priests language.
application:
Spend five minutes simply worshiping today, with no requests. Use the words of 4:8, 4:11, and 5:12.

When you feel that history is out of control, picture the throne and the Lamb holding the scroll.

Think about how Jesus conquered. How might it change how you respond to a situation where you want to win?
prayerPrompts: Worship God as holy, holy, holy.
Thank the Lamb who was slain and has ransomed people for God.
Add your voice to the song of every creature.
